title: Cancer Specialists Still Not Being Taught About Medical Cannabis
description: An article in Medical Express, Gap in oncology training leaves doctors unprepared for cannabis questions, by researchers at Beth Israel Deaconess M...
content_html_sanitized:
An article in Medical Express, Gap in oncology training leaves doctors unprepared for cannabis questions, by researchers at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston reports, “Evidence suggests as many as 40% of adults with cancer turn to marijuana—more properly known as cannabis—to manage symptoms like pain, nausea and anxiety, and many want guidance from their physicians.

 

Yet a new national study led by investigators at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC) finds that most oncologists-in-training, or fellows, feel underprepared to unprepared to manage this increasingly common aspect of their patients' care.”

 

"Patients with cancer are using cannabis, and they're turning to their doctors for advice….. But without high-quality evidence and without structured training, most trainees don't feel equipped to counsel them appropriately."

 

The original study published in the Journal of Cannabis Research, surveyed 189 oncology fellows across 40 training programs in 25 U.S. states. It found that about one in five recommended medical cannabis to more than five patients in the previous year. About one-quarter of fellows had received prior training in medical cannabis, and those with training were twice as likely to recommend it to patients.

 

“They were also significantly more likely to hold informed opinions about its risks, benefits, preferred modes of use, and which cancer patients might benefit most, underscoring the impact education can have on physicians' confidence.”

 

The report is rather disturbing in that it “found that oral ingestion was the most recommended mode of administration”…  “but that current evidence is strongest for cannabis providing relief for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting…”

 

Now, I have never been to medical school, but I would think that vomiting might be a problem for oral ingestion.

 

I can only salute their conclusion, "As medical cannabis becomes more widely used and accepted, it's critical that fellowship training equips future oncologists with the knowledge they need to have informed, thoughtful conversations and support shared decision-making with their patients."

 

However, it is astonishingly late. It has been decades since I first met with some cancer survivors who told me how they could not have endured chemotherapy without having just a few puffs of weed.

 

It’s been thirty years since a daughter called me and told how her father’s oncologist would not discuss cannabis with her.

See Memories of a Good Friday 30 Years Ago

And Another

Good Friday Moment At the NORML Conference. Why I Do This.

 

And it has been almost twenty eight years since Peter McWilliams told me how it helped him cope with AIDS and cancer. His death was probably not avoidable, but he was essentially tortured to death.

See The Murder of Peter McWilliams -- An Indictment, Not an Obituary by Richard Cowan

 

The consequences of the medical profession’s failure to inform themselves and then stand up for their patients has resulted in decades of avoidable suffering and even death.
